extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry, drama, and literary composition (poets, playwrights, critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic diction, metaphor, and plot in tragedy and epic: includes criteria for metaphorical usage, word-formation, diction, unity and structure of plot, metre choice, and the role of the marvelous/irrational. Intended as practical and critical principles for poets and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy / proportion in metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy or proportion is when the second term is to the first as the fourth to the third; we may then use the fourth for the second, or the second for the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can substitute terms across proportional relations (e.g., 'the cup of Dionysus' = 'the shield of Ares'); sometimes qualify the metaphor by adding the term to which the proper word is relative. Even if no word exists for some term, a metaphor may still be used (e.g., 'sowing the god-created light'). Examples and illustrations are given showing how analogy produces apt metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply alien term then deny one of its proper attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: One may apply an alien term and then deny of that term one of its proper attributes (e.g., calling the shield 'the wineless cup').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device permits evocative expressions by combining unfamiliar relational uses while adjusting meaning through denial of an attribute; the passage warns it is an ornamental but legitimate mode of metaphor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly-coined words
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly-coined word is one which has never been even in local use, but is adopted by the poet himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples appear (e.g., certain coinages translated as 'sprouters' or 'supplicator'). Such coinages can be effective but are a distinguishable category of diction to be used with awareness of their novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words as stylistic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is lengthened when its vowel is exchanged for a longer one or when a syllable is inserted; contracted when part is removed; altered when part is unchanged and part re-cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These deviations from the normal idiom produce distinction while preserving perspicuity when used in exceptional cases. They contribute to clearness remote from commonness and should be used sparingly to avoid caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: be clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean: current or proper words make the style clearest but may be mean; unusual words raise the style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An infusion of elements — strange/rare words, metaphorical, lengthened/ornamental forms — is necessary to raise diction above commonplace, but balance is required so clarity is not lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure riddle or pure jargon—balance rare words and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: A style wholly composed of metaphors is a riddle; wholly of strange (or rare) words is a jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither extreme is acceptable: one needs an appropriate mixture so that the diction is distinguished but not unintelligible. Critics who condemn licenses of speech wholesale are in error; moderation and propriety matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in ornamental license
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ ornamental devices (metaphors, rare words, lengthening) with moderation; used obtrusively they become grotesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate insertion of exceptional forms (e.g., in epic) can beautify lines; excessive or purposive ludicrous use produces grotesque effects. Examples compare Aeschylus and Euripides to show how a single word choice alters perceived quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor as highest mark of poetic genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor; this alone cannot be imparted by another and is the mark of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances; it is a skill that distinguishes superior poets and cannot be taught in full by rules alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate word-types by genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different word-types suit different lyric and poetic genres: compound words are best adapted to dithyrambs; rare words to heroic poetry; metaphors to iambic; heroic poetry can employ all varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction that fits the genre: iambic verse reproduces familiar speech and thus favors words common in prose (current/proper, metaphorical, ornamental), whereas heroic (epic) verse tolerates and benefits from rare words and metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action for narrative imitation in single metre (epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot manifestly ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles. It should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic narrative must avoid being merely a sequence of loosely connected events (as in history). Homer succeeds by detaching a single portion and admitting episodes; the work should resemble a living organism and produce the pleasure proper to unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic requires same kinds of parts as tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must have as many kinds as Tragedy: it must be simple, or complex, or 'ethical,' or 'pathetic.' The parts (except song and spectacle) are the same: it requires Reversals, Recognitions, and Scenes of Suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoughts and diction must be artistic. Epic poems can combine these elements and may be simple/complex while maintaining artistic diction and thought (Homer as model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/length limit for epic: bring beginning and end within a single view
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; poems should be on a scale answering in length to the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt a subject too vast to be embraced; choose a portion or limit the theme to avoid over-complication (Homer's practice recommended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic's capacity for simultaneous events & episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry, owing to the narrative form, can present many events simultaneously transacted; these, if relevant, add mass and dignity and relieve satiety with episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simultaneous incidents and episodes to add grandeur and variety; avoid sameness of incident which produces satiety and stage-failure in tragedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of metre: heroic for epic; avoid mixing metres
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic measure has proved its fitness by experience: it is the stateliest and most massive; it most readily admits rare words and metaphors. Mixing different metres is incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer heroic (epic) measure for large-scale narrative. Other metres (iambic, trochaic tetrameter) suit more stirring/action-related verse; do not combine metres inappropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should speak little in his own person
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; he should bring in characters who are each 'with a character of his own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation is primary; the poet's presence should be minimal so as not to obscure the mimetic effect. Homer uses brief prefatory words then lets characters act/speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the wonderful / the irrational with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is required in Tragedy; the irrational (on which the wonderful depends) has wider scope in Epic. The poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities; irrational parts should, if possible, be excluded from the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If irrational elements are introduced they should lie outside the on-stage action (or be given an air of likelihood); once introduced and made plausible, accept them. The poet must veil absurdities with poetic charm; otherwise they become intolerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction placement: elaborate diction in pauses; avoid over-brilliance during character/thought expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. Conversely, character and thought are obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate or elaborate phrasing for moments that do not need to convey character or inner thought; keep dialogue and character speech clear and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative objects and vehicles of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet, being an imitator, must imitate one of three objects: things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be. The vehicle of expression is language—current terms, rare words, or metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the object of imitation and corresponding language vehicle deliberately; there are many modifications of language (current, rare, metaphorical, ornamental) to serve different aims and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities; avoid irrational internal contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities. The tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts; irrationality should be outside the drama's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construct plots depending on internal absurdities; such plots are poor construction. If unavoidable, veil them and render them plausible, but the first choice is to design the plot without them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes and variation to avoid satiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Sameness of incident produces satiety; tragedies fail on stage for lack of variety. Episodes and varying incidents in epic relieve monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce relevant episodes and varying events to diversify a long narrative and maintain audience interest; in drama, confine action to maintain unity while avoiding monotony.
